standard.title: Implement visual programs
standard.description: implement simple algorithms as visual programs involving control structures and input
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can follow and describe algorithms involving sequencing, branching and iteration (AC9TDI4P02). They have described these structures but have not yet implemented them in a programming environment. They have not yet written programs that accept user input.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students implement simple algorithms as visual programs using a block-based or event-sheet environment, including control structures (sequence, branching, fixed-count iteration) and user input.

nodes.label: Writing and running a sequential program
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can write a program that executes steps in order and run it to check it performs as expected
nodes.minimum_width: Write a program with at least three sequential steps, run it, and confirm it performs each step in the correct order
nodes.typical_width: Write and run sequential programs across simple tasks (moving a character, displaying messages, performing calculations); identify what step the program is on when paused
wider: Implement a sequential program that enacts a specific ordered procedure — for example, the strict steps a First Nations ranger follows when handling a specific native animal; discuss why the order must be preserved in the program
Write the same sequential program in two different visual environments (e.g. Scratch and a flowchart tool) and compare how each represents the same logic

response_modes.reason: Writing and running sequential programs is the foundational capability for all subsequent programming work in this descriptor. Students need procedural fluency — the ability to reliably sequence blocks and interpret run output — before branching and input are introduced. Practice and precision here matter more than breadth.

success_criteria: Steps execute in the correct order
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot reliably sequence blocks and run programs cannot add branching or iteration — both require a functioning sequential program as the base. Fluency here is directly prerequisite for N2 and N3.

nodes.label: Adding branching to programs
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can write a program that uses a comparison condition to branch and execute different steps depending on the result
nodes.minimum_width: Write a program with one IF/THEN branch using a comparison (e.g. if temperature > 25) that produces different outputs for different input values
nodes.typical_width: Write programs with comparison-based branches for different contexts — labelling weather as hot or cold, deciding whether to wear sunscreen, responding to a user's answer in a quiz; test the program with values that trigger each path
wider: Implement a program with IF/THEN statements based on a real protocol — for example, IF a specific animal is found injured THEN the ranger follows a specific procedure; discuss how programs can encode decision-making knowledge
Write a program with multiple conditions (IF...ELSE IF...ELSE) for a context with more than two outcomes and explain how each condition is evaluated

response_modes.reason: Students often test their branching program with only one input value and assume it works. Wider task contexts that require testing both branches — and later multiple branches — build the habit of checking conditional logic exhaustively.

success_criteria: Program executes different code depending on the condition value
Both branches produce a correct and distinct output when tested
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who only test one branch path (or don't recognise when a branch fires) produce programs that appear to work but fail on untested inputs — this pattern of partial testing cascades into N4 where combined structures amplify the problem.

nodes.label: Adding iteration to programs
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can write a program that repeats steps a fixed number of times and explain what changes with each repetition
nodes.minimum_width: Write a program that repeats a step a set number of times (e.g. displaying repeated song lyrics, computing a sum using repeated addition); confirm it repeats the correct number of times
nodes.typical_width: Write programs using fixed-count loops for different purposes (repeated display, repeated addition, repeated movement); identify what changes across repetitions and what stays constant
wider: Write a program that uses a loop to process multiple inputs (e.g. asking for a user's name and responding to each) — discuss how loops reduce the need to repeat code manually
Implement a program that uses both a loop and a branch — for example, a loop that counts and branches when a condition is reached; discuss how the structures combine

response_modes.reason: Students who only see loops in one context (e.g. printing repeated text) may not recognise that the same structure applies to movement, calculation and input processing. Multiple task contexts build generalised understanding of iteration as a structure.

success_criteria: Loop executes the correct number of times
Program produces the expected output after the loop completes

nodes.label: Writing programs with user input
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can write a program that takes input from the user or environment and uses it in the program's logic
nodes.minimum_width: Write a program that accepts one piece of user input (e.g. a name or a number) and uses it in the output or a decision
nodes.typical_width: Write programs that take user input or sense environmental input (temperature, location) and use it in decisions or displays; test with different inputs to confirm the program responds correctly
wider: Write a program that takes input from both a user and the environment — for example, combining a user-entered location with a temperature sensor reading to produce a context-specific response
Implement a program where user input modifies iteration — for example, the user enters how many times a step should repeat; discuss how this makes the program more general-purpose

response_modes.reason: User input integrates all three control structures — input values feed into conditions (branching) and can control loops (iteration), all within a sequential program structure. This node is where students coordinate input with previously learned structures, and the coordination is the key learning.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Programs that combine input with branching and iteration across varied contexts offer rich opportunities for students to see how the same structural elements can produce meaningfully different programs. The wider tier (environment sensing, user-controlled iteration) is genuinely generative rather than just harder.
success_criteria: Program reads at least one user or environmental input
The input affects what the program does or displays
